name: The Jevons Paradox
statement: Making a resource cheaper to use can increase, not decrease, how much is used.
meaning: The Jevons paradox holds that when technology makes a resource more efficient to use, cutting the amount needed for any single use, the falling cost of use can raise demand so much that total consumption rises rather than falls. Efficiency gains, meant to conserve a resource, can be offset or even overwhelmed by the extra use they provoke. Jevons put it that to suppose economical use of fuel means diminished consumption is a confusion of ideas — the very contrary is the truth.
mechanism: Improving efficiency lowers the effective price of the service a resource provides — the cost of a mile driven, a lumen of light, a computation. By the law of demand, a lower price raises the quantity demanded, and that extra demand pulls resource consumption back up, the rebound effect. If the rebound is between nothing and full, net consumption still falls, though by less than engineering promised. If the rebound exceeds a hundred per cent — backfire — net consumption rises, which is the Jevons paradox in its strict form.

examples.text: Jevons's original case: Watt's more efficient steam engines made steam power cheaper, so it was adopted across industry and British coal consumption rose rather than fell in the nineteenth century.
Cheaper miles tempt people to drive more, a direct rebound — though empirically this rebound is usually partial, so efficient cars still cut fuel use, just by less than expected.
As compute per task grows cheaper, total demand for it can surge, a modern instance invoked for data centres and artificial intelligence.

variants.name: The rebound effect
variants.text: The general offsetting of efficiency gains by increased use, decomposed into direct rebound in the same service, indirect rebound as savings are spent elsewhere, and economy-wide effects through growth.

variants.name: The Khazzoom-Brookes postulate
variants.text: The modern restatement that economy-wide energy-efficiency improvements increase total energy consumption, named by Harry Saunders in 1992 after Khazzoom and Brookes.

whyItMatters: It is a central caution in energy and climate policy: that efficiency alone may deliver smaller savings than engineering projections suggest, because cheaper use invites more of it. It reframes efficiency not as a guaranteed cut in consumption but as one lever whose effect depends on how demand responds, and it underlies the argument for pairing efficiency with caps or carbon pricing.

working.text: expect real savings from an efficiency measure to fall short of the naive engineering estimate, as cheaper use rebounds.
trace how an efficiency gain lowers the price of a service and how much demand for that service responds.
where the goal is to cut total use, combine efficiency with pricing or caps rather than relying on it alone.

limits: The direction of the mechanism is uncontroversial, but its magnitude is genuinely debated, and the paradox proper requires the rebound to exceed a hundred per cent. Empirical reviews find direct rebound for household energy services in rich countries generally below thirty per cent, so at the micro level efficiency usually does reduce consumption, just by less than promised. Economy-wide backfire is contested and hard to measure: some economists argue macro effects are large, while others find that behavioural and market responses cut intended savings by only a modest fraction. Many hold that full backfire is the exception, not the rule, for individual measures.
misreadings: Efficiency does not always backfire, and it is not pointless — most measured rebound is partial, so efficiency typically still reduces consumption. Conflating a partial rebound of twenty or thirty per cent with full backfire, where consumption actually rises, is a common error; only the latter is the Jevons paradox. And one striking case, whether coal or lighting or computing, does not establish that all or most efficiency gains backfire economy-wide.
origin: Stated by the English economist William Stanley Jevons in 'The Coal Question' (1865), from the observation that more efficient steam engines increased British coal consumption; restated for energy economics in the 1980s as the Khazzoom-Brookes postulate.

sources.text: Jevons paradox, Wikipedia. — the efficiency-raises-consumption statement, the coal history, the rebound and backfire distinction, and the contested magnitude.
Sorrell, Dimitropoulos & Sommerville, "Empirical estimates of the direct rebound effect: A review," Energy Policy 37(4):1356-1371 (2009). — direct rebound generally below thirty per cent.
Gillingham, Kotchen, Rapson & Wagner, "The rebound effect is overplayed," Nature 493:475-476 (2013). — the argument that backfire is not the norm and substantial savings remain.
